input:
It is worth noting that the two lifetime values reported in the literature are, in reality, less far apart than the very different conditions behind them might at first suggest. The first group holds the benchmark material under dry gas at a steady temperature and reports the time taken to reach a fixed loss of capacity, whereas the second group cycles the feed between dry and humid states and reports the time taken to reach exactly the same loss. Under the dry protocol, the material spends its entire life away from the condition that degrades it, and the reported lifetime is, unsurprisingly, correspondingly long. Under cycling conditions, by contrast, water reaches the pore structure on every single cycle, and the loss duly arrives considerably sooner.

The preference expressed here rests, ultimately, on the duty that the material would actually see in service. Where the feed is humid in service, the cycled values describe the life of the benchmark material more closely, and the dry values tend to overstate it. Where the feed is dried upstream and remains dry, the ranking is reversed, and the longer values are the ones that properly apply. It should be noted, however, that neither protocol fully reproduces a real plant feed, in which humidity and temperature move together and neither variable is held steady
